545:// to know it: `{ mounted, declarations, hits, ownerOf }`. Absent - a caller that
546:// only wants the production counters, or an engine too old to resolve the
547:// declarations - the counters that depend on it record no key rather than a zero.
582:// The skills that loaded and were then caught anyway by a check they own. Per
583:// capture file, so the day tier's count is sessions rather than findings - a
584:// session caught three times by one rule is one session the skill did not save.
585:// `ownerOf` maps a rule id to the skill that owns it; without it no key is written.
598:// --- day buckets ---------------------------------------------------------------
600:// An empty day row — the shape every counter folds through. Only the CAPTURE-derived
601:// scalars are zeroed: those are answered by files this fold reads in full every run,
602:// so zero is a fact about the day. Every other day field is left ABSENT until a source
603:// that can answer it does, because a source that could not be read is unknown and a
604:// zero written for it would read as a quiet day.
607:  // Driven off the vocabularies rather than a list here, so a newly appended map
608:  // or group cannot be silently absent from the day tier that feeds the week one.
613:// An empty hour row. All four counters are zeroed: an hour inside the window with no
614:// runs in it genuinely had none — the run listing covers the whole window or the fold
615:// does not advance its watermark at all.
622:// The check maps fold the same way skillLoads do — key-wise, zeros implicit — only
623:// with a fixed-shape counter object under each key instead of a bare number. A
624:// field the group declares as a peak takes the larger of the two rather than their
625:// sum; everything else adds.
636:// Recompute the day rows from scratch, from the live capture files. `files` is
637:// `[{ date, issue, pr, sessionId, counts }]` — one entry per capture file in the raw
638:// window, `counts` being that file's `countEntries` result.
639://
640:// Stateless by construction: a day is a pure function of the files stamped with it,
641:// so there is no ingest ledger, no double-count risk, and a counting-bug fix
642:// self-heals the entire visible window on its next run.
648:  // This capture's session, filed under the day and the name it attests.
654:  // The two PER-SESSION figures, which must not be summed over capture files: a
655:  // session that captured twice (a merge, then the session-end tail) writes the same
656:  // facts into both files, and the second is usually a superset of the first. So they
657:  // are collected per (day, session) and reduced at the end — the largest token spend
658:  // any of the session's captures attests.
670:    // A capture keyed to a PR or an issue has work behind it; issue 0 is a tail
671:    // capture with no merge behind it.
679:    // The two DISTINCT-SESSION counters, which are not sums over capture files: a
680:    // session that captured twice wrote the same facts into both, and both figures
681:    // are rates per session rather than per load or per finding.
688:    // The per-model split rides the SAME winning capture as the total it splits, so
689:    // the two can never describe different captures of one session.
698:    // The task the session belongs to, resolved ACROSS its captures rather than per
699:    // capture: a session has one dispatch, but its captures disagree about the evidence
700:    // — the tail capture is filed under issue 0 where the merge capture named the PR,
701:    // and a capture written mid-run can predate the execution record the tail
702:    // carries. So the most-informed answer any of them gives wins.
705:    // Summed over the session's captures rather than deduped, so the per-task column
706:    // adds up to the day's own `userMessages` scalar, which is summed the same way.
710:  // Distinct sessions, not capture count: one session can capture more than once
711:  // (a merge, then the session-end tail).
713:  // Overwriting rather than adding: the per-file counters above attested presence,
714:  // and what the day carries is how many distinct sessions that came to.
725:      // Absent until one session on this day attested a spend — the fields stay off
726:      // the row entirely on a day whose transcripts carried no usage records, which is
727:      // what makes "this shape does not record it" distinguishable from "it was free".
734:      // Same absence rule for the two wall-clock scalars: a day whose sessions carried
735:      // no entry timestamps keeps no key rather than reporting nobody worked.
740:      // `sessions` and `userMessages` are counted off the capture files and are always
741:      // real; the two token columns stay ABSENT until a session of this task attested a
742:      // spend, so a task whose transcripts record no usage reads as unknown rather than
743:      // as having run for free.
756:// --- the sources outside the capture files ----------------------------------------
758:// Merge a day-keyed map of already-computed fields into the day rows — the shape both
759:// the local-git series (commits and lines) and the releases listing arrive in. A day
760:// the source could not speak for is simply absent from `bySource` and keeps no key,
761:// which is the whole point of doing this outside `emptyDay`.
772:// The queue's own record of what each occurrence came to: closed work items, per task,
773:// per outcome word. APPEND-ONCE past `queueFoldedThrough`, for the same reason the run
774:// ledger is — the items are a paged REST read where the capture files are local git —
775:// and safe to append because a closed item is settled: its outcome label is written at
776:// convergence and nothing later moves it.
777://
778:// `records` is `[{ date, pack, task, outcome, parks }]`, already filtered by the reader
779:// to items that closed past the mark. `parks` is the kinds the item was parked for at
780:// any point in its life, each counted ONCE for it — an item bounced between a person
781:// and the machine twice is one park of that kind, not two — or `null` where the item's
782:// event listing could not be read, which costs its parks and not its outcome.
783:// @deprecated The `queue` and `parks` rows have a successor:
784:// `.claudinite/local/tasks-usage.GENERATED.json`, which counts the same outcomes and
785:// the same parks beside the latencies and costs they belong with
786:// (`packs/claudinite-tasks/tasks/tasks-usage-fold/README.md`). This writer keeps
787:// running — the rows it has already written are real and its readers still read them
788:// — and retiring it is a later plan of its own rather than a window this one closes.
812:// --- merged pull requests ---------------------------------------------------------
814:// What each merged PR took, filed under the day it merged. APPEND-ONCE past
815:// `prsFoldedThrough` for the reason the queue read is: a paged REST resource where the
816:// capture files are local git, and a merge is settled — `merged_at` never moves.
817://
818:// The rows carry DURATIONS, never percentiles: a week's p50 is not the mean of its
819:// days' p50s, so the quantile is the reader's reduction over whatever window it draws
820:// and the fold's job is to carry the sample. `merged` is the key count.
821://
822:// `records` is `[{ date, number, leadHours, issueLeadHours, sessionToMergeHours }]`; a
823:// slot whose far end is unknown is `null` and keeps no key, which is not a zero lead.
841:// --- the hour tier ----------------------------------------------------------------
843:// How long an hour row lives. Three days: long enough for the two-day view the
844:// dashboard draws plus a fold outage, short enough that the tier stays a few dozen
845:// rows rather than a log.
853:// The hour rows for this run. Two sources meeting in one row, and they are kept in
854:// separate FIELDS rather than merged, because they are trued up on different clocks:
855://
856://   - the run counts (`scheduler`, `executor`, `failed`) are APPENDED from the runs
857://     read past the watermark, so prior rows carry forward and are added to;
858://   - the capture-derived counts (`agentic`, and the per-task executions behind the
859://     hover) are RECOMPUTED from the capture files every run, so they overwrite.
860://
861:// Merging them into one counter would make the second source's recompute silently
862:// double the first's appended total.
888:// The capture files' own view of an hour: how many distinct sessions captured in it,
889:// and what they executed. The filename stamp is the clock — the same stamp the logs
890:// branch's retention rules read, machine-written by the capture step.
905:// --- task invocations -----------------------------------------------------------
907:// How long a task row stays in the DAY tier. Independent of the capture retention
908:// on purpose: these rows come from the scheduler's Actions logs, not from the logs
909:// branch, so nothing about them ages out when a capture file does — and a repo that
910:// captured nothing for a week must still show that its scheduled tasks ran. Past
911:// this, the day row goes and its week row carries it, exactly as the capture-derived
912:// days do.
915:// How long a day row lives at all. Wider than the task rows and wider than the capture
916:// retention, because the local-git and queue series reach further back than either and
917:// the growth panels read a month of them. A day past this drops out of the tier; its
918:// week row keeps what it held.
926:// Carry the slot scheduler's task-invocation rows forward while they are still inside
927:// the day window.
928://
929:// HISTORY ONLY, WITH NO WRITER LEFT. These rows counted what the retired slot
930:// scheduler printed into its own Actions log about each due task; that writer is gone
931:// (#974) and its logs have aged out of retention, so nothing appends to them any more
932:// and the reader that did was retired with them rather than left to spend two API
933:// calls a run finding nothing. What each occurrence came to is read from the queue's
934:// own closed items now (`foldQueueOutcomes`), which is the record that replaced it.
935://
936:// So this only ages them out: a day row keeps its `tasks` counts until it leaves the
937:// window, and the week rows that already froze them keep them forever.
947:// --- week buckets --------------------------------------------------------------
949:// The ISO-8601 week a UTC date falls in, `YYYY-Www`. ISO weeks start Monday and
950:// belong to the year containing their Thursday — computed, never approximated,
951:// because an off-by-one here would silently mis-file a whole week's row.
954:  const day = (d.getUTCDay() + 6) % 7;                 // Mon=0 … Sun=6
955:  d.setUTCDate(d.getUTCDate() - day + 3);              // the week's Thursday
964:// The days to fold into weeks this run: every completed day strictly after the
965:// watermark and strictly before today, in order. Days close strictly in order, so a
966:// single monotone watermark is the WHOLE exactly-once mechanism — no ingest ledger.
967:// `today` is excluded because its capture files are still arriving.
974:// Add one day row into its week row, append-once. Weeks carry `days` — how many day
975:// rows they absorbed — so a fold outage longer than the raw retention window
976:// declares its own hole (`days: 5`) instead of silently under-reporting.
977://
978:// `sessionDays` rather than `sessions`: every counter here sums exactly under
979:// folding EXCEPT a distinct-session count (a session spanning two days is distinct
980:// in each), so the week-level field is named for what it actually is — the sum of
981:// the day-level distinct counts — rather than claiming a precision folding cannot
982:// give.
983:// Every scalar add is `?? 0` on the WEEK side for the same reason the counter maps
984:// below default rather than crash: a week frozen before a field existed carries no key
985:// for it, and the field must start accumulating from the first day that has it instead
986:// of wedging the watermark or reading back as NaN.
991:  // Every other week scalar is the sum of the day field of the same name — the two
992:  // exceptions are spelled once, in WEEK_FROM_DAY. Driven off the vocabulary rather
993:  // than a hand-written list so a field appended to both rows folds without a third
994:  // edit here, which is where a new counter would otherwise be silently dropped.
995:  //
996:  // A day with NO opinion on a field adds nothing rather than zero: a week that
997:  // absorbed five days of unreadable git history and two of readable must report the
998:  // two, not seven days' worth of understated lines.
1004:  // The bare maps a week row can carry, so a week frozen before one existed reads
1005:  // back the same shape a fresh fold builds.
1007:  // Every counter group folds key-wise, driven off the vocabulary rather than a
1008:  // hand-written list here — which is where a newly appended group would otherwise be
1009:  // silently dropped out of the week tier.
1010:  //
1011:  // A week frozen before a group existed carries no key for it: defaulted rather than
1012:  // crashed, so the first fold after the group ships extends those weeks from the day
1013:  // it closes forward instead of wedging the watermark behind them.
1014:  //
1019:// --- the whole file ------------------------------------------------------------
1023:// Sorted keys throughout, so a recompute that found nothing new produces a
1024:// byte-identical file and the delivery opens no PR.
1029:// Fold one run: hour rows over the last three days, day rows recomputed from `files`
1030:// (the live raw window), week rows carried forward from `prior` and advanced by every
1031:// day that closed since the watermark. Pure — the caller supplies today's UTC date,
1032:// the prior file, and whatever the outside sources answered.
1033://
1034:// The three tiers answer different questions and are kept honest by different
1035:// mechanisms: hours are for what is happening right now and expire in three days;
1036:// days are cheap to be wrong about (recomputed every run, so a fix heals them); weeks
1037:// are not (frozen once folded — re-freezing would need raw data the retention TTL
1038:// deliberately destroyed), so weeks only ever absorb days that have closed and can no
1039:// longer change.
1046:  // The appended rows are accumulated BEFORE the week fold, so a day that closed since
1047:  // the last run carries them into its week in the same pass that freezes it. (A day
1048:  // whose week is already frozen still shows a late arrival in the day tier — visible
1049:  // there, absent from the week: the same boundary every new counter has, and the same
1050:  // one weeks state for themselves.)
1071:    // How far the queue's own closed items have been read. Its own mark for the same
1072:    // reason the run ledger has one: a different source on a different clock, and one
1073:    // outage must not read as the other's.
1075:    // …and the merged-PR listing's own mark, bounded on `merged_at` for the same
1076:    // reason the queue's is bounded on `closed_at`.
1081:    // The second watermark: how far the scheduler's own run ledger has been read.
1082:    // Separate from `foldedThrough` because it advances on a different clock (runs,
1083:    // not closed days) over a different source, and conflating them would make an
1084:    // outage in one silently look like an outage in the other. Carried forward
1085:    // unchanged when this run read no new runs.
1092:// --- the file boundary ----------------------------------------------------------
1093:// Everything above works in NAMED counters; the on-disk tuple shape is met only here.
1096:// --- the mounted-skill set -----------------------------------------------------
1098:// The skill names this repo mounts, from the PACK REGISTRY — never from
1099:// `.claude/skills/`, which is gitignored session state an Action checkout does not
1100:// carry at all. Fails soft to an empty set: with no mounted set, a typed `/command`
1101:// still counts as a userCommand and simply never counts as a skill load.
1106:// What the mounted corpus offers the counters that need to know it: the skill
1107:// names, the force-load declarations a moment is counted against, the predicates
1108:// that decide whether a moment hit, and which skill owns which check.
1109://
1110:// The engine is probed rather than depended on. Its predicates and the
1111:// `ownerSkill` stamp are newer than this pack's first delivery of these counters,
1112:// and the two lanes land on separate cycles, so every member spends a window
1113:// holding an older engine beside this pack. A namespace import that comes back
1114:// without them leaves `hits`/`ownerOf` unset, and the counters reading them write
1115:// NO KEY - *not recorded*, which is the honest answer, where a zero would report a
1116:// skill whose moments could not be resolved as one whose moments never came.

1	// THE SUBPROCESS PORT. Two things this pack runs outside its own process — the
2	// agent's code-work command, and git — and both are spelled here so `src/` holds
3	// exactly one module that can start one.
4	//
5	// The two shapes are genuinely different and stay separate: code-work is long,
6	// streamed and killable, git is short and read for its stdout. A single
7	// "run a command" helper would have to serve both and would serve neither.
8	
9	import { spawn, execFileSync } from 'node:child_process';
10	
11	// Start a command and stream its output. Returns the child, so the caller owns the
12	// timeout, the kill and whatever it does with the streams — the executor's leash
13	// is policy and does not belong down here.
14	export const startProcess = (command, args, options) => spawn(command, args, options);
15	
16	// Run git and read its stdout. `maxBuffer` is generous on purpose: a generated
17	// file can be large, and a `git show` of one easily tops spawn's default 1 MiB —
18	// which fails as a truncated read, not as an error.
19	//
20	// stdin is 'pipe' exactly when there is input to pipe: an explicit 'ignore' with
21	// an `input` set silently feeds the child NOTHING, and `hash-object --stdin` then
22	// cheerfully writes the empty blob — a wrong answer, not an error.
23	export const runGit = (args, opts = {}) => execFileSync('git', args, {
24	  encoding: 'utf8',
25	  maxBuffer: 256 * 1024 * 1024,
26	  stdio: [opts.input === undefined ? 'ignore' : 'pipe', 'pipe', 'pipe'],
27	  ...opts,
28	});

1	# Tasks usage fold — what the machinery itself cost
2	
3	**This task runs no agent.** It is `agent_model: none` with `code_work: node worker.mjs`, so the whole pass is the deterministic [`worker.mjs`](worker.mjs) the executor runs as code-work, which calls the counting and folding core beside it ([`fold-tasks-usage.mjs`](fold-tasks-usage.mjs)). This file is the human-facing record of what that worker does.
4	
5	## Two files, and why this is not the other one
6	
7	[`usage-fold`](../usage-fold/README.md) folds what this repo's **sessions** did — skill loads, tokens, check findings, what landed in git. This one folds what the **machinery** did: how often the scheduler and the executor ran, what those runs were billed, what they spent in API calls and wall time, and what each occurrence of each task came to.
8	
9	The split is by **source**, not by subject. The session fold's numbers come out of capture files it re-reads for free off a local branch; every source behind this one is a rate-limited REST listing read past a watermark. Keeping them in one file would mean one source's outage degrading the other's rows, one cadence serving two very different read costs, and a single watermark standing for two clocks.
10	
11	What they share is their discipline, deliberately — the same three tiers, the same per-source fail-soft, the same rule that **an absent source leaves no key, never a zero** — and the readers, where one already reads the source: this fold's run listings are [`packs/claudinite-tasks/tasks/usage-fold/read-runs.mjs`](../usage-fold/read-runs.mjs)'s, and its task-and-park decoding is [`packs/claudinite-tasks/tasks/usage-fold/read-queue.mjs`](../usage-fold/read-queue.mjs)'s.
12	
13	## What the file carries
14	
15	`.claudinite/local/tasks-usage.GENERATED.json`, per hour, per day and per week:
16	
17	- **Per workflow** (`scheduler`, `executor`) — `runs`, `jobs`, `minutesBilled`, and `spend`. Actions bills per **job**, not per run, so a run's minutes are the sum over its jobs of each job's wall time rounded up to a whole minute, and the two counts are kept apart. `spend` exists only where this pack's config carries `actionsMinuteRate`: unset leaves **no key at all**, because a public repo bills nothing and a private one bills something, and a zero would be a claim nobody made. The rate every figure was priced at is written into the file beside them, so a rate changed later cannot silently re-price rows frozen under the old one.
18	- **Per run** — `apiCalls` and the wall milliseconds of each phase (`list`, `ask`, `drain` for a tick; `pick`, `claim`, `code-work`, `hand-off`, `converge` for an executor run), from the `claudinite-run-cost` record every run prints. The format is [`packs/claudinite-tasks/src/items/run-record.mjs`](../../src/items/run-record.mjs)'s, beside the two execution records; the API calls are counted at the GitHub port itself, which is the only place every call passes through.
19	- **Per task** — what its occurrences came to (`done`, `delivered`, `obsolete`, `none`), the parks they collected by kind, and four **latency samples** off each closed item's own label events: tick→item, item→pick, pick→hand-off, hand-off→converge. Samples, never quantiles: a week's p50 is not derivable from its days', so the file carries what a reader needs to take the quantile over whatever window it is drawing. A slot whose far end never happened — an agentless item has no hand-off — is absent, which is not a latency of zero.
20	
21	## Where a run's cost record is read from
22	
23	A **scheduler tick owns no work item**, so the record it printed exists nowhere but its job log, and the fold reads it there. That read is what the cadence buys: the scheduler fires twice a day, at most two of its runs have their log read per fold, and at most two jobs are opened per run — so the log reads are bounded at four whatever else happened.
24	
25	An **executor run has items**, so it writes its record where the record survives Actions retention: onto every item it settles, in the same fenced block as the execution record. One run therefore leaves several snapshots of one record, each a reading of counters that only ever grow, and the fold keys them by run id and keeps the **largest** — the run's total as of its last item. Under-counting is one-directional by construction, as every other floor in these two files is.
26	
27	## The API budget
28	
29	Stated here because it is the reason the reads are shaped as they are. Per fold:
30	
31	- two run listings, flat, however many runs are in the window;
32	- one jobs listing per run this fold has not seen;
33	- at most four job-log reads;
34	- one issues listing page, plus one **timeline** read per item closing for the first time — one read, not two, because the timeline carries the labelings, the comments and the close together, which is exactly the three things this fold wants off an item.
35	
36	On this repo's own cadence — two ticks a day and the executor runs a quiet queue dispatches — the run half of that is under ten calls a day, and the task's test asserts it by counting the fetches a representative day makes. `MAX_RUN_READS` is the runaway guard rather than the budget: a day that somehow produced hundreds of runs stops at the cap, leaves the watermark at the last run measured, and says so.
37	
38	## Every tier is appended once
39	
40	This is the one place the discipline differs from the session fold's, and it is worth stating plainly: that file recomputes its day rows from capture files, so a counting fix heals its whole visible window. **Nothing here is recomputed.** Every source is a watermarked listing, a run or an item is folded on the one pass that first sees it, and a counting bug fixed later applies from the fix forward.
41	
42	Appending is safe because each fact is settled once seen — a completed run's start and conclusion do not move, a closed item's outcome label is written at convergence and is never moved — and both watermarks are monotone over those facts, which is the whole exactly-once mechanism. No ingest ledger.
43	
44	Two maps do not reach the week tier on the same terms as the rest. A week's keys are frozen forever, so `runCosts` — keyed by run id, unique per occurrence — is dropped there and its numbers survive as the week's own scalars; per-run detail answers "what did this tick cost", which nobody asks of a week last February. `latency` is kept, unique keys and all, because the samples *are* the week-level answer.
45	
46	## When it runs
47	
48	Daily, and only when the machinery has moved: [`preconditions.mjs`](preconditions.mjs)'s `runs-since-fold` holds while the file's own `runsFoldedThrough` still stands before the scheduler's most recent anchor. That is the mark's own movement rather than standing state — it goes false the moment a fold catches up and true again at the next tick — and it costs no API call, which matters on a term asked at every tick.
49	
50	## The file is GENERATED
51	
52	Machine-written and never hand-edited. It lives under `.claudinite/local/` because that is the repo-owned area the vendoring refresh never touches, and `merge=ours` reaches it through the mount's own `.gitattributes`, whose `*GENERATED*` pattern the engine converges — so this file needed no attributes line of its own.
53

I finished the comment pass on all 16 files in batch2.txt. Every changed line in the .mjs files is a whole-line `//` comment; I checked this by filtering the diff to non-comment, non-blank lines, and nothing remained. No git command that changes state was run.

The most common fix was removing file-name and path mentions, mostly `(PRINCIPLES.md)` / `(docs/PRINCIPLES.md)` pointers and `(xyz.mjs)` references. Next came history and incident stories (who broke what, and when), then comments that repeated the code.

Per file (all under `packs/claudinite-tasks/`):
- **`migrations/2026-08-31-executor-vars-bag/migration.mjs`**: cut the header down to its reasons (the gap for pre-#1494 adopters, why it rewrites instead of copying the stub, why re-runs are safe, why that anchor). Removed the test-file name and how `applyRewrites` works inside, and deleted two comments that repeated `appliesTo`/`legacyPresent`.

- **`queue/tasks/implement-request/README.md`**: removed the "carried over from the declaration's comments" line and the phrase "exactly as every request did before".
- **`src/contract/calendar.mjs`**: shortened the story of the retired `taskScheduler` anchor to its reason (a configurable boundary creates a seam). Removed the doc and file paths and a caller mention (`normalizeTaskDeclaration`).
- **`src/contract/task-declaration-text.mjs`**: replaced a sibling file's name with "lives beside it".
- **`src/contract/task-defaults.mjs`**: corrected a comment that was wrong. It said no field is ever left undefined, but `code_work` and `agent_instructions` are never filled in, so it now says they stay absent and mean none. Also dropped the doc pointer and a comment that repeated the code.
- **`src/schedule/repair-rules.mjs`**:
  - Removed anecdotes: the ClaudiniteCanary cases, missingbulb/TLDR#275, "22 of them", and the #1161/#1253 story.
  - Removed history remarks ("slot grammar", "the old way", "before the beat existed"), the `executor.mjs` path and a "job 1" cross-reference.
  - Fixed a comment naming a `readySince` variable that does not exist.
- **`src/schedule/run.mjs`**: removed about 25 PRINCIPLES.md/file-path mentions. Also removed history: #1373 "reversed an earlier attempt", "pre-heartbeat behaviour", the #1267 list and "this list was the one that did not", the #1354 three-day story, "the only two the merge added", and the "three members at once" story. The #1354 comment now states only why the function is kept out of `main`.
- **`src/session/verify-outcome.mjs`**: removed doc and file pointers.
- **`src/world/git.mjs`**: removed doc and file pointers, the "retired gate / deleted run_daily" history and the settings file name.
- **`src/world/processes.mjs`**: no change.
- **`tasks/tasks-usage-fold/README.md`**: no change.
- **`tasks/usage-fold/corpus-use.mjs`**: removed the file names (`fold-usage.mjs`, `hook-log.mjs`, `session-start-command.sh`, `check-timing.mjs`, `corpus-use.test.mjs`) and kept the reasons for spelling the format locally.
- **`tasks/usage-fold/read-prs.mjs`**: no change.
- **`tasks/usage-fold/read-runs.mjs`**: cut the "predecessor read job logs (#974)" history to the current fact, and removed a file name and a "no longer fetches logs" remark.
- **`tasks/verify-production/probes.mjs`**: no change.

Totals: 195 comment lines removed and 131 written, so about 64 fewer lines, and about 130 lines were rewritten or trimmed. That covers 12 of the 16 files.

diff --git a/packs/claudinite-tasks/src/world/secrets-bag.mjs b/packs/claudinite-tasks/src/world/secrets-bag.mjs
index 7e83dd5..d584ebf 100644
--- a/packs/claudinite-tasks/src/world/secrets-bag.mjs
+++ b/packs/claudinite-tasks/src/world/secrets-bag.mjs
@@ -1,26 +1,14 @@
-// The executor's per-task secret selection (docs/PRINCIPLES.md).
+// The executor's per-task secret selection: a task's code-work gets exactly the names
+// that task declared, selected here, rather than the executor's whole environment.
 //
-// WHAT THIS MODULE IS FOR NOW: making PRINCIPLES.md's claim true. A task's code-work
-// gets exactly the names that task declared, selected here, where before every task's
-// work step inherited the executor's whole environment and saw every stamped secret.
-// That selection is independent of how the secrets arrive, and it is why this module
-// survives the reversal below.
-//
-// THE BAG IS RETIRED (#1336, reversing #1301). The executor briefly carried one static
-// line, `CLAUDINITE_SECRETS: ${{ toJSON(secrets) }}`, so the workflow would stop being
-// a function of the task set — `.github/workflows/` is the one path an update cannot
-// write, and a new secret therefore needs a human-merged PR in every member, which is
-// what wedged one in #1296. But serialising the whole secrets context is the shape
-// GitHub's malicious-workflow detection flags: every executor run parked with zero
-// jobs until a person clicked Approve, silently, fleet-wide. The owner took the
-// trade back — a rare human-merged PR beats a permanent human click on every run.
-//
-// So the workflow names its secrets again and NOTHING SETS THE BAG. The plain
-// environment is therefore the LIVE source, and the bag READER is the tolerance: it
-// stays because a member whose live executor still stamps one moves off it only
-// through a human-merged PR of its own, and dropping the reader early would hand
-// that member's code-work the whole blob, since the scrub in code-work-run.mjs goes
-// with it. Its retirement is a fleet read rather than a canon release (#1914).
+// NOTHING SETS THE BAG (#1336). Serialising the whole secrets context into one

A comment pass over `packs/claudinite-tasks/`, following the rewritten `writing-comment` rule from missingbulb/Claudinite#2324. It covered 100 non-test source files and changed 85; 768 lines were added and 1119 removed.

**Comments that were wrong, now corrected:**
- **`src/session/dispatch.mjs`**:
  - Two comments sat above the wrong function and are moved to the right one.
  - The section header claimed the repair phase re-arms dispatch issues. Nothing outside tests calls those functions, and it now says so.
- **`src/execute/loop.mjs`**: `strikeClaim` described "the roll", which no longer exists; it now describes the requeue.
- **`src/schedule/repair.mjs`**: said "three ops" where there are four.
- **`src/items/usage-format.mjs`**: the `WEEK_FROM_DAY` comment named two special fields where the map has one.
- **`src/contract/task-defaults.mjs`**: claimed no field is ever left undefined, which isn't true of `code_work` and `agent_instructions`.
- **Misc:** `public/delivery.mjs` named a `readAtBase` helper that doesn't exist, and `src/schedule/repair-rules.mjs` named a `readySince` variable that doesn't exist.
- **`worldRules/task-declaration-shape.mjs`**: pointed "above" at a rule that sits below it, and mentioned renames that don't exist.
- **`src/world/secrets-bag.mjs`**: the `secretValue` comment contradicted the module header about which source is live.
- **`tasks/usage-fold/README.md`**: said the task was `agent_model: none`/`code_work`, hourly and a claudinite-growth task. Its `task.json` declares `code_worker_mjs`, runs daily and belongs to claudinite-tasks.

**Removed across the pack:**
- `(docs/PRINCIPLES.md)` and file-path pointers
- change history ("used to", "retired", "(owner, date)", incident stories)
- comments that repeated the code or described how a callee works

Where a comment mixed a real reason with history, the reason stays.

**Checks run:**
- The engine's `commentOnly` comparison passes on every changed code file, so no code changed.
- The `improve-comments-scope` gate is armed by the commit subject and passes.
- Full suite: 4002 pass, 0 fail.

content.text: {"id":"4642507380","url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/2326"}

The comment pass over `claudinite-tasks` is done and ready for review in [missingbulb/Claudinite#2326](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/2326). It covered the 100 non-test source files and changed 85 of them, removing 1119 lines and adding 768. Test files were left out of the pass.

I checked that no code changed: the engine's own comment-only comparison passes on every changed file. The full test suite passes (4002 tests), and the gate that blocks a comment pass from touching code also passes.

**What was cleaned out, in almost every file:**
- Links to `docs/PRINCIPLES.md` and names of other files. Some were garbled, and some pointed at paths that no longer exist.
- History: "used to", "retired", "(owner, date)", and stories about past incidents.
- Comments that restated the code or explained how a called function works.

Where a comment mixed a real reason with history, the reason stayed.

**The more useful finds were comments that were simply wrong.** About a dozen had drifted from the code, and are now corrected:
- **`dispatch.mjs`:** two comments sat above the wrong function. A section header said the repair step re-arms dispatch issues, but nothing outside the tests calls those functions (I checked). It now says so.
- **`loop.mjs`:** described a "roll" that no longer exists.
- **`repair.mjs`:** said "three ops" where there are four.
- **`delivery.mjs` and `repair-rules.mjs`:** named a helper and a variable that don't exist.
- **`task-defaults.mjs`:** claimed no field is ever left undefined, which is false for two of them.
- **`secrets-bag.mjs`:** the comment on one function contradicted the file's own header about where secrets are read from.
- **The usage-fold task's README:** had its setup, how often it runs, and which pack owns it all wrong; I checked each against its declaration.

**Two things to know about how the edits were made:**
- Some subagents edited files through shell scripts instead of the Edit tool. The combined comparison above covers those edits too, but the Stop hook may flag them.
- The pass added long dashes; I replaced every one it added with a hyphen.

Worth deciding separately: three functions in `dispatch.mjs` are now documented as having no caller outside the tests. They could probably be deleted, but that's a code change for its own PR, not this one.

Folders the change touched:
```
packs/claudinite-tasks/public/          comments on the public helpers: pointers, history, restated code removed; wrong helper name fixed
packs/claudinite-tasks/src/             bulk of the pass: history and file pointers cut; comments that had drifted from the code corrected
packs/claudinite-tasks/tasks/           task worker comments trimmed; usage-fold README corrected to match its declaration
packs/claudinite-tasks/queue/           request-implementer comments: garbled pointer fixed, history cut
packs/claudinite-tasks/migrations/      migration notes reduced to the reason each one exists
packs/claudinite-tasks/worldRules/      check comments corrected where they pointed the wrong way
packs/claudinite-tasks/workRules/       file-name mentions removed
```

> ✅ All done

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to re-vendor a repo's mount to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- backfilling-provenance: Filling a pack's empty provenance files from its history. Use when a pack under packs/ or .claudinite/local/packs/ carries empty provenance files, or when asked to backfill or write a pack's provenance.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- changing-pack-elements: What a change to a pack's element owes - the entry on its provenance file, which kind, and how to append it - and what a pack's README carries. Loaded for any edit of a pack's RULES.md, skills, checks, tasks, manifest, README or provenance folder, in a repo's local pack or on a canon's shelf.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- committing: How a commit is cut — one concern per commit, the issue it references, a landed commit revised only by a new one, files staged by name. Use before any git commit.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked `task:origin:ad-hoc` and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- extract-from-instructions: Convert instruction prose somebody already wrote into pack carriers, leaving the prose file a thin routing map. Use when adopting Claudinite on a repo that already carries a CLAUDE.md, when a person wants their machine-local instructions carried properly, or when asked to convert instruction prose into a pack.
- extract-packs-from-a-project: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and author the canon packs those facets earn. Use from a canon when a project's evidence shows a facet its shelf does not yet home — the curation stages' pack-writing method, and an owner's when asking what a project has taught the shelf.
- fetching-from-the-web: Reading a page or a file from the web in a session — exact bytes over a summarizing fetch, and what a 403 or an egress block means. Use before any WebFetch or curl, and when a fetch is denied.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the basics task lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- improve-comments: Improve a repo's own comments as a pass of their own: delete, correct, add the why. Use when working a repo's comments deliberately (the basics pack's improve-comments task), never as a side effect of another change.
- learning-a-technology: Teach a repo a new technology for a job of its own. Use when asked to make a repo do something with a technology nobody there has used yet (host it on X, send through Y, publish to Z), or to "research how to do this correctly" and "create a skill" for it.
- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner approves the current branch or PR, or asks to merge or land it into main.
- production-retrospective: Design and file the review that comes back on its own once a larger element has lived in production. Use when designing a larger element, when filing a migration plan's chain, when a merge completes a design-doc'd element, or when defining a new retrospective class for a pack, a repo, or the fleet.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- revalidating-rules: Re-probe the pack rules whose truth lives outside the repository — harness tool contracts, token reach, whether an MCP tool exists, a platform's behaviour — and correct the ones that have gone stale. Use when a revalidation sweep runs over a corpus of packs, or when asked whether a rule's environmental claim still holds.
- running-the-suite: Running this repo's test suite — the one command that covers it, reading a run's output from a file instead of re-running it, iterating on the tests an edit touches, and staging a new test file before certifying a run. Use before any node --test.
- searching-for-a-tool: Finding a harness tool by name — the select form for a deferred tool, and what an empty search means. Use before any ToolSearch, and when a search finds nothing.
- triaging-usage-findings: Turn a usage-review finding that has lasted into a proposed change - read the element's provenance first, settle which of the rule's causes it is, and write the edit itself rather than a description of it. Use when a usage-triage run hands you lasting findings, or when an owner asks what to do about one.
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- working-with-generated-files: Working with a file a test or tool generates — naming it, changing the generator rather than the file, and resolving its merge conflicts by regenerating. Loaded for any edit of a GENERATED file.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-handover-issues: How to write a task list a PERSON will execute — a handover issue, an adoption checklist, a "steps only a human can do" list. Use when filing or editing any issue whose body asks a human to click, set, register or copy something. Not for issues describing work you will do yourself.
- writing-migration-plans: How a plan's phases are ordered so nothing stalls mid-run. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan (including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file), when asked to run a plan as a chain of ad-hoc tasks, and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-pack-prose: How pack prose is written - RULES.md rules, SKILL.md bodies and check text in a Claudinite pack, local or canon - brevity, structure, triggerability, findability, the marker that names a rule's provenance file. Loaded for any edit of a pack's RULES.md or SKILL.md, and when landing a lesson as prose.
- writing-repo-scanning-checks: How a check that scans the repo picks its file set, strips comments before matching a forbidden token, and proves itself silent against real sources. Loaded for any edit of a coded or declared check.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.json or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever any such runtime behavior would make an artifact more useful, before writing the page.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- workflow-authoring: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
- anthropic-skills:docs: docs (living docs people share, comment on and edit; use only when the user asks for one: names a doc, document, page, memo, spec, PRD, runbook or write-up, asks for somewhere to share or keep editing something, or says yes to your doc offer; a plan, comparison, summary or notes asked in chat stays in chat (at most a one-line doc offer); a report, status update, recap or "something I can send them" with no form named → ask first: reply, doc or file?; tabs hold tables and live charts too; a pasted claude.ai/code/artifact/… link may be a doc: check with docs tools first; not HTML pages, apps or plain chat answers; a .docx/.pptx/.xlsx/PDF asked for by name → that format's skill): asked for one → no docs-connector instructions in context? call the docs connector's `guide` with topic.instructions first, then create the doc (headings only, no body) before any search, file read or plan, even with files attached. - anthropic-skills:docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx) or Word templates (.dotx). Triggers include: any mention of Microsoft Word Documents, such as 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', 'microsoft doc'. ## 2026-09-06 · born · Check that the executor workflow passes every declared secret (#1798)
- **Source:** NoRFinder, whose executor carried an empty secrets list against an endpoint declaring
  a token secret, with two queue items parked needing a human.
- **Reason:** a secret reaches a task only if the executor workflow names it statically, and
  `.github/workflows/` is the one directory a converge may not push to - so the file is scaffolded
  once at adoption and every task or endpoint added afterwards declares a secret the job does not
  carry, with nothing saying so until a run reaches the endpoint call. The expectation is recomputed
  from the same two sources the converge reads, so check and converge cannot hold two opinions;
  extra names are not a finding, since a member that dropped a task keeps a harmless line.
- **Actor:** @missingbulb (owner).
- **Model:** Claude, per the commit trailer.
- **Mechanism:** a world check, `packs/claudinite-tasks/worldRules/executor-workflow-secrets.mjs`,
  advisory rather than blocking: the remedy is a human-merged pull request to `.github/workflows/`,
  the one fix a member's own machinery cannot make, so blocking would turn such a member red with no
  move of its own to clear it.
- **Landed:** #1798 (Closes #1796) · pack version 60906.8.

## 2026-09-06 · reworded · Hold the executor to its tasks' secrets, not the repo's endpoint tokens (#1832)
- **Reason:** the expectation was the union of the tasks' required secrets and every invocation
  endpoint's token secret, but the list the executor must carry is what the tasks of the repo's
  packs require; an endpoint's token is config rather than a task declaration, and the invocation
  call already names a missing one at the moment of the call. Only the check's list narrows - the
  converge keeps stamping the endpoint tokens, so a member's job still carries them.
- **Actor:** @missingbulb (owner).
- **Model:** Claude Opus 5, per the commit trailer.
- **Landed:** #1832 (Refs #1831) · pack version 60906.14.

- **Reason:** the declaration walk the check borrows reads `task.json` alone once the module form is
  gone.

## 2026-09-20 · policy-changed · A task cadence measures whole UTC periods, not a per-repo anchor (#2182)
- **Reason:** `taskScheduler.dailyHour` and its siblings let a repo move the boundaries a cadence
  was measured against, which put a seam inside every day: before the anchor hour the current period
  was still yesterday's, so one run read as consumed at 03:00 and as open at 09:00. A period is now
  the UTC calendar and nothing else, and the term says out loud what it is, a rate limit on the
  scheduler's own asking rather than a claim that there is work to do. A corpus-wide decision, cited
  here.
- **Actor:** @missingbulb (owner).
- **Model:** Claude Opus 5, per the commit trailer.
- **Mechanism:** the declaration's `due:daily` precondition becomes `schedule:at-most-daily`; the
  gate on real work is still `unreleased-commits` beside it.
- **Landed:** #2182 (Closes #1995) · pack version 60920.3.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to re-vendor a repo's mount to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- backfilling-provenance: Filling a pack's empty provenance files from its history. Use when a pack under packs/ or .claudinite/local/packs/ carries empty provenance files, or when asked to backfill or write a pack's provenance.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- changing-pack-elements: What a change to a pack's element owes - the entry on its provenance file, which kind, and how to append it - and what a pack's README carries. Loaded for any edit of a pack's RULES.md, skills, checks, tasks, manifest, README or provenance folder, in a repo's local pack or on a canon's shelf.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- committing: How a commit is cut — one concern per commit, the issue it references, a landed commit revised only by a new one, files staged by name. Use before any git commit.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked `task:origin:ad-hoc` and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- extract-from-instructions: Convert instruction prose somebody already wrote into pack carriers, leaving the prose file a thin routing map. Use when adopting Claudinite on a repo that already carries a CLAUDE.md, when a person wants their machine-local instructions carried properly, or when asked to convert instruction prose into a pack.
- extract-packs-from-a-project: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and author the canon packs those facets earn. Use from a canon when a project's evidence shows a facet its shelf does not yet home — the curation stages' pack-writing method, and an owner's when asking what a project has taught the shelf.
- fetching-from-the-web: Reading a page or a file from the web in a session — exact bytes over a summarizing fetch, and what a 403 or an egress block means. Use before any WebFetch or curl, and when a fetch is denied.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the basics task lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- improve-comments: Improve a repo's own comments as a pass of their own: delete, correct, add the why. Use when working a repo's comments deliberately (the basics pack's improve-comments task), never as a side effect of another change.
- learning-a-technology: Teach a repo a new technology for a job of its own. Use when asked to make a repo do something with a technology nobody there has used yet (host it on X, send through Y, publish to Z), or to "research how to do this correctly" and "create a skill" for it.
- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner approves the current branch or PR, or asks to merge or land it into main.
- production-retrospective: Design and file the review that comes back on its own once a larger element has lived in production. Use when designing a larger element, when filing a migration plan's chain, when a merge completes a design-doc'd element, or when defining a new retrospective class for a pack, a repo, or the fleet.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- revalidating-rules: Re-probe the pack rules whose truth lives outside the repository — harness tool contracts, token reach, whether an MCP tool exists, a platform's behaviour — and correct the ones that have gone stale. Use when a revalidation sweep runs over a corpus of packs, or when asked whether a rule's environmental claim still holds.
- running-the-suite: Running this repo's test suite — the one command that covers it, reading a run's output from a file instead of re-running it, iterating on the tests an edit touches, and staging a new test file before certifying a run. Use before any node --test.
- searching-for-a-tool: Finding a harness tool by name — the select form for a deferred tool, and what an empty search means. Use before any ToolSearch, and when a search finds nothing.
- triaging-usage-findings: Turn a usage-review finding that has lasted into a proposed change - read the element's provenance first, settle which of the rule's causes it is, and write the edit itself rather than a description of it. Use when a usage-triage run hands you lasting findings, or when an owner asks what to do about one.
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- working-with-generated-files: Working with a file a test or tool generates — naming it, changing the generator rather than the file, and resolving its merge conflicts by regenerating. Loaded for any edit of a GENERATED file.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-handover-issues: How to write a task list a PERSON will execute — a handover issue, an adoption checklist, a "steps only a human can do" list. Use when filing or editing any issue whose body asks a human to click, set, register or copy something. Not for issues describing work you will do yourself.
- writing-migration-plans: How a plan's phases are ordered so nothing stalls mid-run. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan (including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file), when asked to run a plan as a chain of ad-hoc tasks, and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-pack-prose: How pack prose is written - RULES.md rules, SKILL.md bodies and check text in a Claudinite pack, local or canon - brevity, structure, triggerability, findability, the marker that names a rule's provenance file. Loaded for any edit of a pack's RULES.md or SKILL.md, and when landing a lesson as prose.
- writing-repo-scanning-checks: How a check that scans the repo picks its file set, strips comments before matching a forbidden token, and proves itself silent against real sources. Loaded for any edit of a coded or declared check.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.json or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. - artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
